creator: Tom Kwiatkowski, Jennimaria Palomaki, Olivia Redfield, Michael Collins, Ankur Parikh, Chris Alberti, Danielle Epstein, Illia Polosukhin, Jacob Devlin, Kenton Lee, Kristina Toutanova, Llion Jones, Matthew Kelcey, Ming-Wei Chang, Andrew M. Dai, Jakob Uszkoreit, Quoc Le, Slav Petrov (Google Research)
description: Natural Questions (NQ) is a question answering dataset where questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. An annotator is presented with a question along with a Wikipedia page from the top 5 search results, and annotates a long answer (typically a paragraph) and a short answer (one or more entities) if present on the page, or marks null if no long/short answer is present. The public release consists of 307,373 training examples with single annotations, 7,830 examples with 5-way annotations for development data, and 7,842 examples with 5-way annotations sequestered as test data.
name: Natural Questions
rai:annotationsPerItem: Training examples have 1 annotation each; development and test examples have 5 annotations each (5-way annotation). A subset of 302 examples has 25-way annotations for analysis.
rai:annotatorDemographics: A pool of around 50 annotators, with an average annotation time of 80 seconds per item.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Post-hoc evaluation of annotation quality was performed by four expert annotators (the first four authors) who independently classified a sample of 139 examples into Correct (C), Correct but debatable (Cd), and Wrong (W) categories, then reached consensus. Long answer precision was 90% and short answer precision was 84%. Additionally, 25-way annotations on 302 examples were collected to study variability; the most popular long answer accounts for 83% of annotations, and the two most popular account for 96%.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators are presented with a (question, Wikipedia page) pair and complete three stages: (1) Question Identification — determine if the question is good (fact-seeking) or bad (ambiguous, incomprehensible, opinion-seeking, etc.); (2) Long Answer Identification — select the earliest HTML bounding box (paragraph, table, list item, or whole list) containing enough information to infer the answer, or mark 'no answer'; (3) Short Answer Identification — select the entity or set of entities within the long answer that answer the question, or flag yes/no/no short answer possible. Comprehensive guidelines were developed and annotation quality was constantly monitored.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset focuses exclusively on Wikipedia as the evidence source, which may introduce biases. The authors acknowledge this choice and note that future data collection efforts may introduce other domains. Questions are limited to those of 8+ words, focusing on longer, more complex queries. The question heuristics exclude 'how to' questions.
rai:dataCollection: Questions are real anonymized, aggregated queries of 8 or more words issued to the Google search engine by multiple users in a short period of time. Queries are filtered using heuristics to retain fact-seeking questions. Each question is run through Google search and kept only if a Wikipedia page appears in the top 5 results. The resulting (question, Wikipedia page) pairs are then presented to human annotators for answer annotation.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine (queries of 8 words or more issued by multiple users in a short period of time), paired with Wikipedia pages from the top 5 search results.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is limited to Wikipedia as the evidence source. Questions are restricted to those of 8+ words, excluding shorter queries and 'how to' questions. There is genuine ambiguity in whether answers are acceptable for naturally occurring questions, and multiple valid answers often exist. The dataset focuses on single-turn QA, not conversational QA.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Heuristic filters are applied to the query stream to retain fact-seeking questions of 8+ words. Filters include syntactic patterns (e.g., questions starting with 'who', 'when', 'where' followed by specific verb forms, questions containing multiple entities with adjectives/adverbs, etc.). Part-of-speech tags and entities are identified using Google's Cloud NLP API. Questions are further filtered to keep only those with a Wikipedia page in the top 5 Google search results.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is designed to have genuine utility to users as open-domain question answering has significant utility, and a solution to NQ will have genuine utility as a benchmark for NLU. The authors argue that closing the gap between baseline systems and human performance will require significant advances in NLU.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmark for question answering research; training and evaluation of end-to-end QA systems; driving research in natural language understanding; studying human performance in providing QA annotations for naturally occurring questions.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Google's Cloud NLP API (used to identify part-of-speech tags and entities during question filtering)

null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not explicitly discuss missing data handling beyond the NULL answer labels which are part of the task design, not missing data.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific timeframe for data collection is mentioned in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described; NULL answers are a designed part of the task, not imputed values.
null_reasons.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: No post-collection data manipulation, augmentation, or resampling is described for the dataset itself.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan is described in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The paper explicitly states questions are anonymized; no personal or sensitive information is discussed as being collected.

evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: 307,373 training examples with single annotations; 7,830 examples with 5-way annotations for development data; and a further 7,842 examples with 5-way annotated sequestered as test data. We present experiments validating quality of the data. We also describe analysis of 25-way annotations on 302 examples.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The guidelines and tooling divide the annotation task into three conceptual stages, where all three stages are completed by a single annotator in succession. Question Identification: Contributors determine whether the given question is good or bad. Long Answer Identification: For good questions only, annotators select the earliest HTML bounding box containing enough information for a reader to completely infer the answer to the question. Short Answer Identification: For examples with long answers, annotators select the entity or set of entities within the long answer that answer the question.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Annotation is performed using a custom annotation interface, by a pool of around 50 annotators, with an average annotation time of 80 seconds.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotation is performed using a custom annotation interface, by a pool of around 50 annotators, with an average annotation time of 80 seconds.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Post hoc evaluation of non-null answers leads directly to a measure of annotation precision. Long/short answers have 90%/84% precision, respectively. We also describe analysis of 25-way annotations on 302 examples, giving insights into human variability on the annotation task.
evidence.rai:dataCollection: All the questions in NQ are queries of 8 words or more that have been issued to the Google search engine by multiple users in a short period of time. We run questions through the Google search engine and keep those where there is a Wikipedia page in the top 5 search results. The (question, Wikipedia page) pairs are the input to the human annotation task described next.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. All the questions in NQ are queries of 8 words or more that have been issued to the Google search engine by multiple users in a short period of time.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: All the questions in NQ are queries of 8 words or more that have been issued to the Google search engine by multiple users in a short period of time. We run questions through the Google search engine and keep those where there is a Wikipedia page in the top 5 search results. Annotation is performed using a custom annotation interface, by a pool of around 50 annotators.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: From these queries, we sample a subset that either: 1. start with ''who'', ''when'', or ''where'' directly followed by: a) a finite form of ''do'' or a modal verb; or b) a finite form of ''be'' or ''have'' with a verb in some later position... Part of speech tags and entities are identified using Google's Cloud NLP API: https://cloud.google.com/natural-language.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Part of speech tags and entities are identified using Google's Cloud NLP API: https://cloud.google.com/natural-language.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: We focus on Wikipedia as it is a very important source of factual information, and we believe that stylistically it is similar to other sources of factual information on the Web; however, like any data set there may be biases in this choice. Future data-collection efforts may introduce shorter queries, ''how to'' questions, or domains other than Wikipedia.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: We focus on Wikipedia as it is a very important source of factual information, and we believe that stylistically it is similar to other sources of factual information on the Web; however, like any data set there may be biases in this choice. Future data-collection efforts may introduce shorter queries, ''how to'' questions, or domains other than Wikipedia.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: Our goals are three-fold: 1) To provide large-scale end-to-end training data for the QA problem. 2) To provide a data set that drives research in natural language understanding. 3) To study human performance in providing QA annotations for naturally occurring questions.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Open-domain question answering (QA) is a benchmark task in natural language understanding (NLU), which has significant utility to users, and in addition is potentially a challenge task that can drive the development of methods for NLU. We also believe that, because a solution to NQ will have genuine utility, it is better equipped as a benchmark for NLU.
